text: The Signal Dial (GluD Receptors): So if NMDA is the spark, is anything else turning the signal up or down? Well according to a recent finding by Johns Hopkins researchers, GluD receptors, until now known for helping build synapses, are channels in their own right, and what opens them is D-serine (one of the tools below) and GABA, the brain's calming chemical, rather than glutamate (Wang, et al, 2025). What has been measured in people so far all points one way: the channel sticks open and leaks, so the synapse never gets quiet. That is what the mutation behind one inherited ataxia does, and a gene variant that raises the risk of schizophrenia does the same (Allen, et al, 2023). So my guess for the armored state is that it jams the dial the same way, stuck part-way on, which is what hyper-vigilance would be at the level of one synapse: a floor the signal can't drop below. Nobody has tested that in trauma yet, and it can be tested, because a drug that shuts these leaking channels already works in the lab.
reader: someone with trauma armor who is about to take NAC, zinc, magnesium, L-serine or D-serine to calm a glutamate storm and to make therapy sessions stick, and wants to know what each one actually does

checked.point: in an armored state the dial jams High (ataxia, hyper-vigilance) or Low (apathy, schizotypy)
checked.found: what is measured in people is a channel stuck open: the ataxia mutation, and a schizophrenia-risk variant of GluD1 (Allen 2023). Nothing puts apathy or schizotypy on a "Low" setting
checked.still_needed: yes for the High side, as his hypothesis with its mechanism; no for the Low side
